newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-BUBA MOVES TO CAP DOLLAR, SAYS ECONOMY SOUND.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BUBA MOVES TO CAP DOLLAR, SAYS ECONOMY SOUND.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Wednesday launched a fresh verbal attack on the robust dollar, but at the same time made clear that the mark's return to a lower level was having a positive impact on the German economy.
In its February monthly report, the Bundesbank said the mark appreciation seen in early 1995 -- when the dollar fell to an all-time low of 1.3438 marks -- had now more than reversed.
"The strong appreciation from the start of 1995 has been more than corrected in the meantime," the central bank said.
The message conveyed in the Bundesbank's monthly oracle was also immediately reinforced by President Hans Tietmeyer, who told a German newspaper the dollar should now stop rising.
"I hope that this correction has now come to an end," the mass-circulation Bild quoted him as saying.

The dollar, which last year staged a steady recovery from its 1995 record lows, has surged around 10 percent since the start of the year. The dollar on Wednesday was trading at about 1.69 marks in European dealings.
Apparently anxious that the market psychology of a stronger dollar could drift unnoticed into a weak mark policy, the Bundesbank has intervened verbally to support the mark several times this month.
A weak mark could destabilise the economy by pushing up import prices which in turn creates domestic inflation.

But the central bank admitted in its report that the dollar's strength had also had a positive impact on the German economy -- boosting its exports -- and had so far had no negative impact on inflation.

The economic outlook remained good even though growth had dwindled to zero in the final 1996 quarter, the Bundesbank said, citing the positive impact of low wage rises, better currency levels and low interest rates.

"The stimulus within the German economy did not continue towards the end of 1996," the Bundesbank said. "However the calming in economic activity is not to be seen as the same thing as a change in the trend."

But the Bundesbank sent warnings to the Bonn government on the need to rein in its budget spending to give Germany access to European monetary union and on the urgent need for structural reform to cut record unemployment.
The bank said Germany's chances of meeting the criteria for entry to the euro would depend on how Bonn overcame pressures from record employment that weighed on the 1996 budget.
"Whether the estimated budget deficit can be sustained in the final analysis will depend upon to what extent additional burdens can be compensated for," the report said.

The Bundesbank called on Bonn to make every effort possible to control spending during the year, noting the government has raised its 1997 deficit forecast to 2.9 percent from an earlier forecast of 2.5 percent in November 1996.

Acknowledging that record unemployment remained Germany's greatest economic problem, the Bundesbank urged the federal government to implement clear reforms to counter this as soon as possible, saying monetary policy was powerless to help.

It welcomed government steps to improve the competitiveness of German companies through tax reform and reform of welfare payment systems and urged Bonn to implement such reforms quickly to help stimulate investment.
"The current economic problems in Germany, which are overwhelmingly structural in origin, can only be solved by economic and political reforms and not with a policy of cheap money," it said.

Noting that investment was the weakest element in the current upturn, it said: "The early creation of certainty (on reform) could help considerably to increase the willingness of companies to invest and thus to create new jobs."
Reinforcing recent statements from council members that no policy changes were on the cards, the report made clear the Bundesbank saw no reason to lower interest rates any time soon.
At the same time it recognised that inflation was low, giving no cause for a rate increase. It blamed a rise in annual inflation to 1.8 percent in January on special factors.
Economists generally expect no interest rate changes from the Bundesbank's regular meeting on Thursday.
